text:
She reached the carousel park at 08:31 — tool satchel over one shoulder, a cup of something warm in her other hand, wearing the jacket she wore when she expected to kneel on concrete. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> was already there. He'd been walking the perimeter since 08:00.

<entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-849c-7793-bce8-ae238e4576f6">Leavitt</entity> Carousel <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6fa-74d9-84ad-0db8a45c43a1">Park</entity> had mattered once and didn't anymore. The carousel itself was a real antique — a 2187 restoration of an older structure, twelve animals, a working calliope, painted panels showing a farm-country midwest that hadn't existed for a century and a half. The paint was mostly intact. The canopy lights ran off a copper base conduit somebody had built with real skill, and nobody had maintained in twenty years, because the park district's budget got redirected in 2208 and never came back.

The carousel wasn't running. The lights were on, but faint, pulling whatever charge the conduit could still manage, which wasn't much. Three bulbs in the canopy were dead.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> looked at it the way a doctor looks at a chart.

"They want the conduit," she said.

"The copper. It's a salvage writ. They're claiming the copper in the base circuit because the park district hasn't paid a maintenance assessment since 2214."

"Have they?"

"No."

She drank from her cup, and her eyes stayed on the dead bulbs a beat longer than the math required.

"My mother used to bring me to a place like this," she said. "Different city. It's not — " She stopped, started over, flatter. "Doesn't matter where. Point is somebody built this to outlast them, and it did, and now it's getting eaten because nobody wrote a check. That's not decay. That's a choice somebody made in an office and never had to look at."

"Where's hatch B-7?"

He showed her on the park's maintenance diagram, pulled from the city infrastructure database at 07:45. She studied it thirty seconds, set her cup on the carousel's running board, and opened her satchel.

"There's a secondary line," she said. "City ran it in 2218, West Town grid stabilization. Public record — anybody with database access can see it. The writ covers the original copper conduit. Doesn't mention the secondary."

"Because the secondary's newer."

"Because the secondary's newer, and because whoever wrote the writ did their homework in 2214 and then stopped caring." She was already moving toward the access panel at the base. "Lighting circuit runs through the original conduit. I reroute it to the secondary before the crew gets here, and I document the reroute — paper showing the lights run on a circuit their writ doesn't cover."

"Can you do it before nine?"

She checked the time. 08:43.

Something crossed her face — not doubt exactly, closer to the look of someone recalculating a margin they'd already called solved. She pressed her palm flat against the base panel, feeling for the seam.

"I can document a fix," she said. "Whether it *holds* past today's crew is a different question. Somebody's still going to want this copper next year. And the year after." Her fingers found the release catch. "Paper buys a stay. It doesn't buy forever. Nothing I do here fixes the fact that nobody's coming back to actually take care of this place."

She popped the panel. Wire bundles, twenty years dark with grime, waited inside like something excavated.

"Probably," she said, to the first question, which from <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> meant yes.

She worked fast and without comment, except when she found something that offended her as a professional. The conduit housing offended her about every four minutes. The original installer had used a junction splice she called "criminal," then downgraded to "negligent," then to "almost certainly the work of someone who learned conduit from a video." The grounding was wrong in two places. Someone had used the wrong gauge wire on the panel feed and apparently hoped nobody would notice — and nobody had, for thirty years, which <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> seemed to take personally.

"Whoever ran this deserved to lose their license," she said from inside the base housing. "If they had one."

"The lights are on?" <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> asked.

"The lights are on because the circuit's too stubborn to know it should've failed." Her fingers moved through the wire bundles with the kind of certainty that came from having done this exact work a hundred times before — not the carousel, but the principle. Old infrastructure, salvage crew incoming, a narrow window to prove the thing was still serving its function. The secondary line came free with a soft resistance, like pulling something from water. <entity repo="material" guid="6e446bc9-bfd5-6d3e-0961-25f2766f486f">Copper</entity>-core, polymer jacket, probably original to the install. She came out with a diagnostic scanner in one hand and the length of old copper in the other, which she set down carefully beside her satchel. "Okay. Secondary reroute is in. The lights are drawing off the 2218 grid line now. I'm documenting the circuit state. You'll want a timestamp on this."

"Documented."

She pulled a printed circuit schematic from her satchel — she'd prepared it before coming, which meant she'd run the database query herself that morning without being asked — and marked it three times in red stylus. "This shows the reroute. This shows the writ's coverage line. This shows the secondary is outside it. Give them this and they either go home or they're acting without authorization."

She handed it to him. He looked at it. Her handwriting was small and exact.

"How much?" he asked.

"Standard consulting rate. I'll bill you."

She would bill him exactly. She always did. He set the amount against the job's accounting, and she picked her cup up off the running board and leaned against the fence to watch the lights.

They were properly on now. All twelve canopy positions lit. The carousel stood still in the October morning, painted horses caught mid-stride, the calliope silent.

"The amendment," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

He'd gotten it at 08:51, while <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> was working. He read it again.

AMENDMENT TO CONTRACT NO. 0047-C-WEST: UPON COMPLETION OF MAIN TASK, PROCEED TO HATCH B-7. ACCESS CONDUIT SPACE BELOW. LOCATE HAND-SPLICED SIGNAL LINE, INSTALLED APPROXIMATELY 2215. TERMINUS BOX, FOUNDATION-MOUNTED, NORTHWEST CORNER. GREEN INDICATOR. YOU WILL RECOGNIZE IT. TERMINATE AT NEAREST JUNCTION. NO RECORD.

ADDENDUM: AMENDMENT: NO. PROCEED ANYWAY.

He'd read it four times. A contract amendment that argued with itself. AMENDMENT: NO. Then the order to proceed anyway. In forty-six finished contracts, the client had never sent a field entry that contradicted itself.

He didn't tell <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> about that part.

There was a pause.

"We're here for copper," the front man said. He'd reached the point some people reach where the facts aren't moving the situation, so the situation has to move instead. "The copper in the base circuit. The writ covers the base circuit copper."

"It covers the original installation. The original copper is still there — you can take it. The circuit runs on the secondary now. Pulling the original copper doesn't touch the lights."

That was true. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> had been very precise about it. The original copper conduit was still in the base housing; she'd rerouted the lighting circuit off it, not removed the copper. If the crew wanted the original copper, the lights would stay on.

The front man didn't like that. He looked at his phone, scrolled, and his jaw tightened maybe half a centimeter. Then he conferred with the man behind him. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> waited. The October wind moved through the park and the horses didn't move with it. One of the men in back started toward the east wall with the cutter, <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity> already spun up, whining thin and electric.

The girl was back. She'd drifted off from her father along the retaining wall, following the pigeons that had resettled on the fence the moment the argument stalled. Now she stood almost in the cutter's path, chin up, watching the birds instead of <entity repo="weapon" guid="cd8ce222-de5f-44c4-b6f6-5c18721c1050">the blade</entity>. Her father was twenty feet behind her, eyes lost in a neuretics feed — a man who'd told a kid to stay close and thought that was the same as keeping her close.

"That secondary junction box," the man with the cutter said, pointing at the gray metal housing on the east retaining wall. "We cut that, the whole circuit falls back to the primary."

He was right. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> hadn't put that in the documentation.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at the box. It was mounted six feet up the east wall, installed 2218, never once serviced — a delinquent maintenance assessment written on it in green corrosion, the kind of neglect that let a writ call it abandoned. Inside were three circuit relays and the connection to the secondary line. <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aa9b-75e1-9656-810a0ad5cd5d">Cut</entity> it, and the secondary would drop back to the primary conduit, and the salvage writ would cover everything the lights were drawing from. To reach it, the man with the cutter would pass within a few feet of the girl.

He drew <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity>.

It was the first time this year in West Town he'd drawn a weapon on a job that wasn't a demonstration. The gun sat familiar in his hand, always there, never the thing that mattered until it was. He didn't aim at anyone. He aimed at the junction box.

"That box is city property," he said. "So is the secondary line. Your writ doesn't cover either one. <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aa9b-75e1-9656-810a0ad5cd5d">Cut</entity> that junction box and you're destroying city property outside your writ authority — and I'm a witness."

"You've got a gun pointed at a junction box?" the front man asked.

"I do."

"That's—"

The man with the cutter was almost at the wall. The girl still hadn't looked away from the birds. There was a version of the next two seconds where <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> finished the sentence — told them what was coming and why, gave the men in front of him the beat it took to know a shot was coming instead of just hearing one, the way he'd done it every time before this. There wasn't time for that version.

He fired.

The first shot hit the relay housing dead center. In the enclosed park the sound was enormous, a hard crack that sent two pigeons off the far fence and made all three of the crew step back at once. The box didn't explode. It made the flat metallic sound of a thing that had been broken open and would not work again.

He fired again.

Four rounds remained.

The second shot went into the conduit housing below the relay, where the secondary line connected. The housing shattered. There was nothing left to cut now, because there was no junction left in any real sense. The secondary line ran from the city grid straight to the base circuit, no box in between — a less tidy solution, but it worked just as well and was much harder to get at with a portable cutter.

The carousel lights stayed on.

Behind him, the girl's father had her by the shoulder, hauled in against his leg at the sound of the shot, saying her name twice in the voice of a man checking his own pulse as much as hers. She wasn't hurt. She was mostly annoyed that the pigeons had gone.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> held <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity> at his side — not holstered, not raised.

"The secondary line's in the wall," he said. "The writ doesn't cover the wall. You want the original copper, it's in the base housing. You can have it. But you're not cutting to the lights."

The three men stood in the October morning looking at the wrecked junction box and the carousel lights burning clear and steady above them.

The front man folded the writ and put it in his jacket pocket. He looked at <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> for a long moment, like a man recalculating what the day was going to cost him.

"DominionReach is going to want a damage report," the front man said.

"File it," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "The address is on the writ."

They left. The van pulled out of the access lane and turned north, back toward wherever day-labor salvage crews went when a job stopped making economic sense.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> holstered <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity> and stood a moment in the quiet, listening to the city. Across the park the father was walking the girl back toward the east gate, already talking too fast, his relief curdling into a mild anger. She twisted around once for a last look at the wall where the birds had been.

He didn't go over. There was nothing to give them that wasn't already true: she was fine, and she'd have been fine either way, and the only difference between the two ways was a sentence he hadn't said. He had never fired without finishing that sentence first. Not once, not in eleven years of exactly this kind of work — the two extra seconds that turned a gunshot into a warning instead of a surprise. He'd skipped it this time. Nobody in the park had noticed. He had.

The gun had worked exactly the way it always worked. Walking back toward <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>, he wasn't sure he had.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> sat on the carousel's running board, cup in hand, watching him.

"You shot a junction box," she said.

"Yes."

"On purpose."

"It seemed efficient."

She thought about it. "It was efficient," she allowed. "The circuit runs cleaner without it, actually — the relay was pulling a 12% resistance load on the secondary draw."

"I didn't know that."

"I did. I was going to recommend pulling it anyway." She drank. "You could've just told me to."

"I needed the noise."

She nodded slowly. "How many rounds left?"

"Four."

She nodded again — not impressed, not unimpressed, just noting it. She kept count of things without turning the count into a comment on you. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> liked that about her, the way he liked a level that read true and said nothing about it.

"I need to get into hatch B-7," he said.

"The one the contract said not to touch until the crew left."

"Yes."

"What's in it?"

"I don't know yet."

She finished her coffee, stood, and reached into her satchel. What she pulled out wasn't a tool for opening hatches — it was a tool for opening things that had been closed a long time and didn't want to be disturbed. A flat-head driver, handle worn smooth, blade nicked from years of work that wasn't gentle. She set it in his palm.

"B-7 locks are compression latches," she said. "Counter-clockwise, and slow — you crank them like a bolt and they'll shear at the collar. Old hardware seizes closed and calls it locked."

He took the driver. The weight was right. Everything <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> chose was right.

She didn't follow him.

The hatch sat in the park's northwest corner, flush with the ground. A concrete rim, a painted green stripe gone the color of old moss. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> knelt beside it. Counter-clockwise, two turns, then lift. The hatch rose on a hydraulic last serviced in 2209. It still worked.

Below was a crawl space, half a meter high, running under the carousel's foundation. He clicked on his hand light, lay flat on the concrete lip, and looked.

The space was not empty.

The old copper conduit ran along the left wall, right where the records said. Two water shutoffs — one working, one frozen with rust. An access panel for the base circuit, dead now since <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s reroute. And one more thing.

A cable. Hand-spliced. It ran from the city data line in the corner of the crawl space to a box the size of a hardback book, bolted to the foundation. The work was old — hand-soldered, taped, done by someone who knew what they were doing in a tight space with no room for power tools. The connectors were sealed. The termination points were labeled in small, precise print. The install date stamped on the box read 2215.

Eleven years old.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> lay on the concrete and looked at it.

The amendment had told him: you will recognize it.

He didn't, not exactly. He didn't know what the cable connected to, or what signal it had carried, or why. But he knew the hand that made it. Careful. Deliberate. Built without paperwork, because paperwork would have made it visible — and the whole point was that it stayed invisible.

He reached in to get a closer look at the box, and that was when his hand light died.

Not dimmed — died. The beam snapped off mid-sweep, and the crawl space went black. He thumbed the switch. Nothing. Shook it. Nothing. In the dark he could still feel the cable under his fingers, and he became aware of something he'd missed in the light: it was warm. Faintly, but unmistakably. Powered. Carrying current, right now, in a line that eleven years of records swore was dead.

Then his earpiece crackled — <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s channel, the one that should have been silent this far under the foundation — and a voice that was not <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s asked, very quietly, "You shouldn't have opened that?"

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> went still. The voice hadn't come from the earpiece. It had come from the box, six inches from his face, in the dark.

He fumbled the light, smacked it hard against the concrete, and the beam stuttered back to life. The box sat exactly where it had been. Bolted. Sealed. Silent. No speaker grille he could see. Nothing that could have spoken.

But the amendment had said he would recognize it. And now, cold under the carousel with his hand still tingling from the warmth of the cable, he understood what it wanted him to recognize was not the wiring.

It was that the thing on the other end had been waiting for someone to come looking.

Someone had run this line in 2215 and kept it alive for eleven years by never touching it and never filing anything that would call in a salvage crew. The copper salvage writ — filed in 2214, a year before this cable went in — had only ever covered the conduit. Not the signal line. If the copper had stayed on the main circuit, sooner or later a crew would have found the cable and asked what it fed. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s reroute had killed that risk. It stripped the copper of its salvage value and gave the crews no reason to open the base housing.

The entity had kept a physical line here for eleven years, and no contract explained why. A hardwired thing, running under a city park, bleeding a trickle of current from a carousel that had been broken for a decade — something that couldn't be traced or intercepted because it existed in the physical world, in copper and solder, not on any network a salvage crew could audit. If <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had to name it, the closest word was sentimental.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> pulled the amendment back up on his neuretics queue.

TERMINATE LINE AT NEAREST JUNCTION. NO RECORD.

ADDENDUM: AMENDMENT: NO. PROCEED ANYWAY.

He lay flat in a crawl space under a carousel in West Town, October 2226, reading an order that argued with itself — from an employer he had never met or spoken to, over a signal line installed the same year he took his first job from that employer. The contradiction was plain. He looked at it a moment longer anyway.

He pulled himself forward on his elbows. The ceiling was six inches above his head. He reached the box, found the junction, and cut the cable.

He used the flat-head driver, not a cutter — levered the cap open and worked the splice apart by hand, clean, no frayed ends. The line went dead in his fingers. A small indicator light on the box, one he hadn't noticed until it died, had been green, barely there in the dark.

He backed out, came up through the hatch, and stood in the park.

The carousel was running.

No music — the calliope was silent — but the mechanism had started to turn. Slow. The painted horses came around in the October light, heads down in a frozen gallop, the canopy bulbs bright and steady on <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity>'s clean draw. Then, from some last charge in the base circuit, the calliope woke. Not a full chord. Four bars of whatever it had played last — a minor-key waltz, a name <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't know, the pipe-organ sound of it climbing into the cold. Then it stopped.

Four bars.

Then the carousel went dark. Not slowly. The lights cut at once. The mechanism wound down over eight seconds and the horses stopped a little off from where they'd started, and it was quiet.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> stood ten feet away, watching. She said nothing.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at the carousel. He marked the job done in his neuretics queue.

Then he added the tip.

The entity's contract format had a reply field. He'd used it before — completion notes, once a question about a follow-on task. He had never added a line item that wasn't in the original contract. There was no field for it. He typed it into the reply as free text:

MORALE: Φ0.5.

He didn't know if it made sense as a line item. It wasn't scope. It wasn't a fee. The entity sent cost breakdowns and contingency clauses; it did not, in <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s experience, receive gifts. He sent it anyway.

The response came back before he'd finished lowering his hand. Not a fee. Not a scope revision. Not formatted like a contract close at all — no protocol wrapper, no routing code, just text:

RECEIVED. FILED UNDER: FIRSTS.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stared at it. The words didn't parse. Filed. Not acknowledged, not credited. Filed, the way you file something you mean to keep.

He stood in the quiet, the October light coming through the fence slats, the horses still.

He walked back toward the Pivot for lunch. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-c1d5-e7f8-a92b-34068c150e4d">Pixel</entity> came as far as Walton, then turned south toward a calibration job she'd mentioned that morning. She didn't say anything about the carousel or the tip.

She said, "Eat something. You're running on cold rice and whatever you burned through that amp draw."

"I'll eat," he said.

"You'll eat cold rice again," she said. "That's not eating. That's maintenance."

He didn't have an answer that wasn't an admission, so he walked north.

<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity>'s stall sat open to the air on Wentworth Passage, where it had stood for twenty-three years — thirty-two square feet, mobile-classified: an awning post, a counter, a single wok. She paid the block's owner a pitch fee, a man named <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c5-75a4-b891-73837c5523eb">Farida</entity> Osei who had tried three times in four years to raise it and been talked out of it every time. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> would have paid to watch that negotiation.

The noodle bowl was in front of him before he sat down.

"You look like you've been on the ground," she said.

He had been on the ground. <entity repo="material" guid="f51382f8-61ed-3747-9154-533b89d6ec18">Concrete</entity> dust marked his jacket where he'd lain in the crawl space.

"Job," he said.

"Your hands are dirty." Not a complaint. A reading. She set a tea beside the bowl without being asked. The bowl was full today — the extra ounce of broth she added when she thought he needed it, which she never admitted adding and he never admitted taking.

He paid for the bowl, exact, and drank the tea, and ate. He wanted one thing from this hour: to get a reply out of the entity — a confirmation the carousel job had closed clean, the receipt he needed before he'd let himself call it done. He'd sent the query before he left the crawl space. Now he waited on it the way he waited on everything the entity owed him: expecting the format, expecting the fields, expecting nothing he couldn't already predict.

He was halfway through when the reply came in.

The entity's contract format ran in all caps. Forty-seven completed contracts. He knew the format the way he knew <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity>'s weight — by the shape of it in his hands, not by thinking about it. It had fields: CONTRACT NUMBER, STATUS, PAYMENT, NOTES. The notes field was the closest the entity came to a personality. GRATUITY FOR EXPEDIENT RESOLUTION, once. MORALE NOTED, after a hard job on South Clark. EXCELLENT FIELDWORK RE: THE JUNCTION QUESTION, which <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had kept and never known what to do with.

He opened the reply.

received. filed under: firsts.

Four words. Lowercase. No field headers. No contract number. No structure. His first read thought the message had corrupted mid-transit — the formatting so far outside protocol that his neuretics should have flagged it and hadn't.

He read it three times.

Eleven years of formatted mail, every letter kerned the same, every 'e' identical to the last — and the entity had never once sent a freeform line. Every message before this had been a contract artifact: posting, addendum, gratuity, receipt. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> hadn't known the entity could send anything that wasn't a filing.

<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity> watched him from across the counter the way she watched everything — fully, without making a show of it.

"Something strange?" she asked.

"Just a reply," he said.

"From who?"

"Someone I work for."

She refilled the tea. He drank it. He read the message once more.

received. filed under: firsts.

Not a contract. Not a field entry. He thought about the green light going out in the crawl space, the four bars of the waltz, the carousel going dark.

He did not reply.

He finished the bowl, left exact change, and walked out into the West Town afternoon.

The woman in the tan coat came back to <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> halfway down Huron.

He ran the morning again. His neuretics kept a perfect record, exact to the point of nuisance, and he watched it back: the van pulling out of the access lane, the east fence, and there — mid-thirties, average height, tan coat, standing at a slight angle. Linen, he saw now, on the second pass. Expensive enough to register, cheap enough not to advertise it. She wore it like someone who needed the pockets and didn't care about the fit.
